english: Consorts, concubines, princes and royal grandsons, bidding farewell to their towers and palaces, were carried by carriage to Qin;
singing at dawn and stringed at night, they became the ladies of the Qin palaces.
Those glimmering stars are the mirrors of makeup being opened;
those green clouds in swirling disorder are the morning tresses being combed;
the greasy swell of the Wei River is the cast-off scented water;
the slanting smoke and drifting mist is pepper and orchid burning.
The sudden thunderclap is the palace carriages passing;
their rumble fading afar, vanishing none knew where.
Every limb, every mien, rendered to the utmost of grace and beauty; standing long in gazing afar, hoping for favour.
Some never saw him even in thirty-six years.
The treasures gathered of Yan and Zhao, the riches amassed of Han and Wei, the treasures collected of Qi and Chu, plundered from their peoples through generations, were piled like mountains.
Once they could no longer be kept, they were carted here.
Tripods treated as pots, jade as stone, gold as clods, pearls as gravel—scattered and strewn along the way, the men of Qin regarded them with no great pity.
One man's heart is the same as the heart of ten thousand men.
Qin loved pomp and extravagance, yet the people too cherished their own homes.
Why, in taking, did they scrape even the smallest grain, and in spending squander it like mud and sand?
The pillars bearing the roof outnumbered the farmers in the southern fields;
the rafters of the beams outnumbered the weavers at their looms;
the glistening nail-heads outnumbered the grains of millet in the granaries;
the uneven tile-seams outnumbered the threads of silk on one's own body;
straight rails and cross bars outnumbered the city walls of the Nine Regions;
the hoarse strains of pipes and strings outnumbered the speech of people in the markets.
So the people of the empire dared not speak, yet dared to be angry.
The heart of the solitary tyrant grew daily more arrogant and obstinate.
Garrison soldiers cried out, Hangu Pass was taken, the men of Chu with one torch—alas, a pit of scorched earth!
He who destroyed the Six States was the Six States themselves, not Qin.
He who exterminated the Qin clan was Qin itself, not the world.
Had the Six States each loved their people, they would have been enough to resist Qin.
Had Qin again loved the people of the Six States, it could have passed down through three generations to ten thousand, and who could have destroyed its line?
The men of Qin had no time to mourn themselves, so later men mourned them.
If later men mourn them yet fail to learn from them, they will make still later men mourn them in turn.
The Six States fell not because their weapons were dull nor their fighting poor, but because their ruin lay in bribing Qin.
Bribing Qin drained their strength—that was the road to destruction.
Some say: all six states perished one after another—was it all because of bribing Qin?
The answer: those who did not bribe were lost because of those who did; deprived of strong allies, they could not survive alone.
Hence it is said: the fatal flaw lay in bribing Qin.
Beyond what Qin won by attack, it gained towns in small measure and cities in large.
Compare what Qin obtained this way with what it won in battle: the former was a hundredfold.
What the feudal lords lost this way, compared with what they lost in defeat, was likewise a hundredfold.
So Qin's great desire and the lords' great peril lay not on the battlefield.
Think of their forefathers, braving frost and dew, cutting through thorns and brambles, to win these few feet of land.
Their heirs held them of little worth, handing them over to others like discarding a blade of grass.
Today cutting five cities, tomorrow ten, and only then gaining a single night's sound sleep.
Rising to scan the four borders, there came Qin's armies again.
Thus the lords' land was limited, but Insistent Qin's appetite was insatiable; the more they fed it, the fiercer it pressed them.
Hence, without fighting, victory and defeat, strength and weakness were already decided.
As for utter overthrow, reason made it indeed inevitable.
The ancients said: "Serving Qin with land is like carrying firewood to put out a fire; while the firewood is not spent, the fire is not quenched."
This saying hit the mark.
